questions.prompt: Kadane's algorithm finds the maximum-sum contiguous subarray in:
questions.explanation: It scans once, at each element deciding whether to extend the current subarray or start fresh, keeping a running best. This dynamic-programming-in-disguise runs in linear time with O(1) space.

questions.prompt: The word-break problem (can a string be segmented into dictionary words?) is solved by DP in:

options.text: O(n^2) time, checking each prefix boundary against the dictionary

questions.explanation: dp[i] is true if some j < i has dp[j] true and the substring from j to i is a word, giving O(n^2) checks (times word-lookup cost). The naive recursion without memoisation is exponential.

questions.prompt: In the house-robber problem (maximum non-adjacent sum), each state depends on:

options.text: A sorted order of house values
The choice to rob the current house plus dp two back, or skip it and take dp one back

questions.explanation: dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], dp[i-2] + value[i]) captures the adjacency constraint, and only two prior values are needed so space is O(1). It is the archetype of constant-space linear DP.

questions.prompt: The partition problem (split a set into two equal-sum halves) reduces to which classic DP?

options.text: Subset sum, targeting half the total

questions.explanation: If any subset sums to half the total, the rest forms the other half, so it is a subset-sum decision with target sum/2. This is pseudo-polynomial in the total sum.

questions.prompt: The coin-change problem of counting the number of ways to make an amount is order-independent. To avoid counting permutations, the DP loop order should be:

options.text: Outer loop over coins, inner loop over amounts
Outer loop over amounts, inner loop over coins
Both loops in any order give the same result

questions.explanation: Fixing a coin in the outer loop ensures each combination is counted once, in a canonical coin order. Swapping the loops counts ordered sequences, which is the different minimum-coins or permutation variant.

questions.prompt: The maximum-product subarray problem differs from the maximum-sum version because it must also track:

options.text: The minimum product so far, since a negative times a negative can become the new maximum

questions.explanation: A large negative product can flip to a large positive when multiplied by another negative, so both the running max and min must be maintained. Kadane's sum version needs no such second quantity.

questions.prompt: The number of distinct ways to climb n stairs taking 1 or 2 steps equals:
questions.explanation: Ways(n) = Ways(n-1) + Ways(n-2), which is the Fibonacci recurrence. It is computed in O(n) time and O(1) space with two rolling variables.

questions.prompt: The 'jump game' of reaching the last index, where each value is a maximum jump length, has an O(n) solution using:

options.text: Depth-first search of all jump sequences
A greedy scan tracking the farthest index reachable so far
A full O(n^2) DP with no faster option

questions.explanation: Maintaining the farthest reachable index and failing if the current index exceeds it decides reachability in one pass. The greedy insight beats the straightforward quadratic DP.

questions.prompt: Why is memoisation essential in the recursive solution to the longest common subsequence?

options.text: Without it, overlapping subproblems are recomputed, giving exponential time
It reduces the space to zero

questions.explanation: The same (i, j) subproblems recur across many branches, so caching each once collapses the exponential tree to O(mn). This is the defining benefit of dynamic programming.

questions.prompt: The 0/1 knapsack DP can be flattened to a 1-D array if the inner capacity loop iterates:

options.text: In any direction with the same result
From low capacity up to the maximum
From high capacity down to the item weight, so each item is used at most once

questions.explanation: Iterating capacities downward ensures each item's contribution reads a value not yet updated for this item, enforcing the 0/1 constraint. Iterating upward instead allows reuse, which is the unbounded-knapsack variant.
